body.heading: Every ping is a small tax
paragraphs: A notification does not need to be opened to cost you something. The glance, the decision about whether it matters, the half-formed reply in your head — each one spends a little of the attention you were saving for something else.
Individually these taxes are tiny. Across a day of ordinary phone use, they add up to a feeling many people know well: busy all day, and unsure what actually got done.

body.heading: Batch, do not ban
paragraphs: You do not have to choose between total silence and total noise. A middle path works well: turn off alerts for everything except the genuinely urgent — calls from family, perhaps — and let the rest wait in a queue you check at chosen times.
Three or four checking times a day suits most people: mid-morning, after lunch, late afternoon. Messages still get answered the same day; they just stop interrupting every hour of it.

body.heading: Tell people what you are doing
paragraphs: The fear that drives constant checking is usually social: someone might need me. So say the quiet part out loud. Tell close people, “I check messages a few times a day — ring me if it is urgent.” Almost everyone is fine with this, and many quietly copy it.
Then notice what the quieter hours feel like. For most people there is a short restless patch, and then a calm they had forgotten was available.

takeaway: Let the noise arrive in batches, at times you choose, instead of drop by drop all day.
